article_title: Lenses on Literature — Evidence for ESSA
citation: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org
title: Sequenced literacy units organized around a Driving Task Prompt moving through comprehension, knowledge building, genre study, synthesis, and writing
description: This pattern organizes curriculum units and modules around a Driving Task Prompt within a disciplinary-literacy framework. Students explore complex, diverse texts through a sequenced instructional journey that includes comprehension, knowledge building, genre study, synthesis, and writing. The design purposefully builds knowledge and supports text-based analysis and communication across genres and formats.
requirements: Units require complex, diverse texts and standards-aligned rubrics for embedded formative assessment of performance tasks.
examples: Teachers implemented at least two Lenses modules in history/social studies or science in the Kentucky study.
key_sources: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org

article_title: Preschool Quality and Child Development: How Are Learning Gains Related to Program Ratings?
citation: Sussman, J., Melnick, H., Newton, E., Kriener-Althen, K., Draney, K., Mangione, P., & Gochyyev, P. (2022). Preschool quality and child development: How are learning gains related to program ratings? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/422.974
title: Desired Results Developmental Profile (DRDP) teacher-administered developmental assessment
description: The DRDP is a developmental assessment administered by children's classroom teachers, completed based on teacher and family observations in five essential readiness domains: social and emotional development, language and literacy development, mathematics, approaches to learning–self-regulation, and physical development. It is completed in fall and spring, providing a measure of children's learning and development over the preschool year. The article reports the assessment is valid for formative and summative assessment with diverse groups of children, including multilingual learners, children with disabilities, and children from different racial/ethnic groups.
requirements: Teachers collect documentation about observed developmental competencies over a 6-week period before making item ratings
constraints: As an observational assessment, it might be subject to concern about teachers' reliability as assessors
target_learners: preschool children, including multilingual learners and children with disabilities
examples: Fall and spring DRDP scaled scores in three domains served as outcomes in the study's regression models
key_sources: Sussman, J., Melnick, H., Newton, E., Kriener-Althen, K., Draney, K., Mangione, P., & Gochyyev, P. (2022). Preschool quality and child development: How are learning gains related to program ratings? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/422.974

article_title: The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors
citation: Li Lucy, Albert Zhang, Nathan Anderson, Ryan Knight, Kyle Lo. (2026). The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00925
title: DrawEduMath benchmark of teacher-annotated student hand-drawn math responses
description: DrawEduMath is an English-language benchmark pairing 2,030 images of real K-12 students' handwritten responses to math problems with three data types: 2.0k+ free-form teacher captions, 44.4k+ synthetic QA pairs, and 11.6k+ teacher-written QA pairs. It draws from the ASSISTments platform and a taxonomy the paper simplifies into image creation and medium, correctness & errors, and content description question types. The authors describe it as involving "noisy, naturalistic data pulled from an online learning platform," and use it to snapshot 11 VLMs' performance.
requirements: Teacher annotations and QA pairs from experienced teachers
An LLM-as-judge scoring setup (majority vote of Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o) to binarize answer similarity
constraints: Single English-language benchmark from one platform (ASSISTments); estimated 85% of images from Title I schools; questions reflect what was salient to Teaching Lab annotators
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving and error diagnosis
examples: Evaluation of 11 VLMs released in 2025 across four developers, with a leaderboard continuously updated for a year after release
key_sources: Li Lucy, Albert Zhang, Nathan Anderson, Ryan Knight, Kyle Lo. (2026). The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00925

article_title: DraftTrace: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing
citation: Divyansh Chandarana, Sandipan De, Vivek Gupta. (2026). DRAFTTRACE: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36544
title: DRAFTTRACE multi-view writing analytics environment
description: DRAFTTRACE is a web application (React front end, Express back end, PostgreSQL store) that captures writing events with timestamps and input channels, records interactions with an integrated AI assistant proxied through the server, and reconstructs documents after submission. After submission, "DRAFTTRACEreplays the recorded events to rebuild the document and labels each character by how it entered: typed, inserted from the built-in assistant, pasted with or without a cited source, or unknown." It organizes analytics at submission, longitudinal, and class levels for instructors, and integrates with LMSs.
requirements: Students complete assignments within the DRAFTTRACE editor so that editing events and AI interactions are captured
Instructors configure the level of AI assistance per assignment
constraints: It captures activity occurring within its writing environment and cannot observe all external resources or activities that may contribute to a response
target_learning_goals: instructor understanding of how student writing was produced
examples: Deployed in a graduate NLP course with 81 students; the system prompt instructs the assistant to support understanding rather than write answers.
key_sources: Divyansh Chandarana, Sandipan De, Vivek Gupta. (2026). DRAFTTRACE: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36544

article_title: Know When to Trust: Making AI Scoring More Reliable for Educational Assessment
citation: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1
title: Use self-confidence, weighted probabilistic scoring, and ensembles as drop-in improvements to existing LLM-based educational scoring systems
description: The article recommends adopting its three techniques as drop-in additions to existing LLM scoring pipelines: "All three techniques improve the performance and trustworthiness of automated scoring models, and are compatible as drop-in improvements to existing techniques." It positions them for systems that derive a quantitative measure from text input.
requirements: An existing LLM-based scoring system that derives a quantitative measure from a text input
constraints: The article's evidence base is scoring of divergent thinking responses (the Alternative Uses Test)
target_learning_goals: reliable automated scoring of open-ended divergent thinking responses
examples: The techniques were tested on over 20,000 Alternative Uses Test responses from more than 2,000 participants across multiple studies, improving correlation with human judges from r = 0.781 to r = 0.823
key_sources: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Draft differences and version history practices foregrounding developmental accountability across drafts
description: Draft comparison practices invite learners to compare selected versions of their work to explain what changed, what role GenAI played at different stages, and how revisions improved clarity, accuracy, or alignment with disciplinary criteria. The paper frames this as "developmental accountability": learners demonstrate responsibility not by producing a single untainted artefact but by showing how evaluative decisions evolved across drafts. Version history functions as an integrity artefact capturing learning trajectories.
requirements: Expectations for specificity, justification, and alignment with disciplinary criteria help mitigate the risk of selective self-presentation
constraints: The emphasis is on purposeful reflection on moments of learning and judgement, not exhaustive tracking; grading attends to progression and coherence rather than quantity of revisions
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI across drafting stages
target_learning_goals: articulating how evaluative judgement evolved across revisions
examples: Early drafts may reflect substantial technological scaffolding during ideation, while later revisions increasingly reflect learner agency and disciplinary understanding
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Dramaturgies of Deception: AI Humanizers and the Performance of Legitimacy in Higher Education Assessment
citation: Roe, J., Perkins, M., Bannister, P., Furze, L., & Wood, J. (2026). Dramaturgies of Deception: AI Humanizers and the Performance of Legitimacy in Higher Education Assessment. A preprint.
title: Dramaturgical framework (front stage, back stage, leakage) with a four-criterion scoring rubric for analyzing commercial misconduct services
description: The article operationalizes Goffman's dramaturgy for analyzing commercial AI misconduct services, defining a front stage in which "a carefully constructed performance is curated", a back stage where "the reality and underlying architecture of the performance are obscured", and leakage where the mask slips. It develops a scoring rubric mapping four criteria (visibility and reach, persona, trust and authority artifacts, mystification) onto front-stage performance, each scored 1-5, and an MCDA rubric extending this to text, image, and layout. The authors offer this as a methodological template extending beyond humanizers specifically.
requirements: Audience-accessible pages must be analyzable as a bounded performance from site access to exit
constraints: The rubric was not designated as a positivist measurement instrument but as a conceptual, structured framework; inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's alpha of 0.48) was moderate
Only publicly visible front-stage content is analyzable; backstage operations are concealed
target_learning_goals: critical analysis of commercial AI services
examples: Three pilot websites were independently scored and calibrated using Krippendorff's alpha before the full analysis of 55 sites
key_sources: Roe, J., Perkins, M., Bannister, P., Furze, L., & Wood, J. (2026). Dramaturgies of Deception: AI Humanizers and the Performance of Legitimacy in Higher Education Assessment. A preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02649

article_title: Examining the efficiency of schedules of distributed retrieval practice
citation: Pyc, M. A., & Rawson, K. A. (2007). Examining the efficiency of schedules of distributed retrieval practice. Memory & Cognition, 35(8), 1917-1927. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03193420
title: Discontinue practice with items once they are correctly recalled, but only after a sufficiently long initial interval between study and first practice test
description: This principle implements a dropout (variable) test-restudy schedule: items correctly recalled during a practice test are removed from the practice stack so remaining trials go to unlearned items. The article shows this yields "levels of memory similar to those obtained with conventional schedules of learning" while using significantly fewer trials — but only when the initial interstimulus interval was long (23 items); a 5-item initial interval dropout schedule produced lower final recall. The authors mirror the flashcard strategy students already report using spontaneously.
requirements: Practice must combine retrieval (test) with restudy of the answer on each trial.
The interval between initial study and the first test-restudy trial must be long enough that items are no longer readily available in working memory.
constraints: Evidence comes from Swahili-English paired associates with a 40-min retention interval; the authors state that "the efficiency of dropout schedules with more complex materials and longer test delays should be established before strong, general recommendations can be made."
Dropping recalled items incurred a measurable cost relative to a long-ISI conventional schedule (23-23-23) in Experiment 2, offset by gains on initially incorrect items.
target_learning_goals: efficient allocation of limited study time
examples: In Experiment 1 and 2, items correctly recalled on a test-restudy trial were removed from the to-be-learned list, and freed trials were allocated to initially incorrect items, which received up to six trials.
key_sources: Pyc, M. A., & Rawson, K. A. (2007). Examining the efficiency of schedules of distributed retrieval practice. Memory & Cognition, 35(8), 1917-1927. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03193420

article_title: Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial
citation: Matthew Barr. (2017). Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.016
title: Drop-in game lab structure preserving flexible play sessions for ecological validity
description: The study's delivery pattern was a supervised lab open on a drop-in basis (9am-5pm Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays) where students managed their own play time within a prescribed per-game log target. The author argues this "partially addresses a common criticism of laboratory-based video game studies", because an arbitrarily defined time limit on play does not mirror normal play circumstances, and that "the lab was arranged to provide better ecological validity" than a rigid temporal structure.
requirements: Participants take responsibility for their own time management within prescribed play targets
constraints: Even this relaxed drop-in structure is not an accurate reflection of how games are played at home
target_learning_goals: graduate skills development through game play
examples: Students could play for "just 5 min more" or leave for a class, and sometimes played longer than prescribed at natural stopping points such as completing a level
key_sources: Matthew Barr. (2017). Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.016

article_title: Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science
citation: Aridor, K., Dvir, M., Tsybulsky, D., & Ben-Zvi, D. (2023). Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science. Instr Sci, 51, 729–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09626-8
title: DReaM framework: nine sub-categories of uncertainty articulations integrating statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty
description: DReaM (Deterministic Relativistic and Middle ground) is an integrative framework offered by the authors that organizes learners' uncertainty articulations into nine sub-categories spanning three reasoning domains. The article states: 'Based on literature from the three fields of statistics, science and nature of science education, we offer an integrative framework, Deterministic Relativistic and Middle ground (DReaM), which consists of nine sub-categories of uncertainty articulations.'
requirements: Learners engage in activities designed to concurrently foster statistical, scientific and nature of science reasoning
constraints: Framework elaborated through a single instrumental case study of two middle school students
target_learning_goals: coordinating statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainties
examples: Used to analyze a pair of middle school students' participation in the Radon Citizen Science Project learning sequence
key_sources: Aridor, K., Dvir, M., Tsybulsky, D., & Ben-Zvi, D. (2023). Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science. Instr Sci, 51, 729–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09626-8

article_title: Stimulating teachers’ equity literacy through drama and theatre-based work forms: A systematic review
citation: Meedendorp, E., & Deunk, M. (2025). Stimulating teachers’ equity literacy through drama and theatre-based work forms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100664. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100664
title: Taxonomy of drama and theatre-based work forms: embodiment, prompted drama, stepping in, and collective play building
description: The review organises the drama and theatre-based work forms found in its 26 included articles into a four-branch taxonomy. As printed, "The drama and theatre-based work forms could be categorised as work forms focused on embodiment, prompted drama, stepping in, and collective play building." The categories emerged from the data analysis rather than being imposed a priori, and they describe distinct ways of structuring dramatic activity in teacher education to provoke critical reflection on equity and diversity.
requirements: Work forms must be drama or theatre-based activities used in pre-service or in-service teacher education to elicit critical reflection among teachers.
constraints: The taxonomy emerged from the 26 articles included in this review; applicability beyond that corpus is not established in the source.
target_learning_goals: critical reflection on diversity and inclusion
examples: The review categorised the work forms reported across the 26 included articles into the four named branches.
key_sources: Meedendorp, E., & Deunk, M. (2025). Stimulating teachers’ equity literacy through drama and theatre-based work forms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100664. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100664

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: Driver diagrams as a collaborative tool for building working theories of AIEd improvement
description: A driver diagram is a visual IS tool the article recommends for AIEd improvement work: "Driver diagrams include a measurable aim, primary drivers that directly impact the aim, and secondary drivers that localize change to specific parts of a system of practice." Primary drivers are described as "a representation of a community's hypothesis about the main areas of influence necessary to advance the improvement aim"; secondary drivers serve as starting points for developing, testing, and refining change ideas.
requirements: Construction as a collaborative tool bringing together multiple perspectives of the program
A measurable aim, primary drivers, and secondary drivers
constraints: Drivers are hypotheses built from research and context-specific data, and primary drivers are often too general to lead to focused change ideas
target_learners: Teachers and AIEd researchers co-developing improvement aims
target_learning_goals: Building working theories of practice improvement for AIEd systems
key_sources: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8

article_title: Drawingvoice 2.0: classroom joint designing and Facebook interactions to develop reflexivity and awareness
citation: Carnevale, S., Di Napoli, I., Esposito, F., & Arcidiacono, C. (2021). Drawingvoice 2.0: classroom joint designing and Facebook interactions to develop reflexivity and awareness. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 2939–2962. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10042-3
title: Small-group joint drawing followed by discussion in a larger multimedia group
description: Each exercise was "characterized by discussion and joint design in small groups and a subsequent discussion in a larger multimedia group". Classroom work in small groups of maximum 3–6 participants produced 12 drawings in Exercise I and 8 in Exercise II, which were then shared and discussed at the whole-class and online level. The structure is reusable wherever joint visual production needs to be aggregated into whole-group reflection.
requirements: Small groups of maximum 3–6 participants
A facilitator to manage the small comparison groups, which are changed in various steps
examples: Exercise I produced 12 drawings and Exercise II produced 8 drawings from the small groups
key_sources: Carnevale, S., Di Napoli, I., Esposito, F., & Arcidiacono, C. (2021). Drawingvoice 2.0: classroom joint designing and Facebook interactions to develop reflexivity and awareness. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 2939–2962. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10042-3

article_title: Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies
citation: Pyle, K. K., & Fabiano, G. A. (2017). Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies. Manuscript submitted to Exceptional Children October 2016; accepted March 2017.
title: Daily Report Card (DRC) as a stand-alone behavioral intervention for students with ADHD
description: The DRC is a behavioral intervention in which "The DRC is an operationalized list of a child's target behaviors (e.g., interrupting, noncompliance, academic productivity)" with "specific criteria for meeting each behavioral goal". Teachers "provide immediate feedback to the child regarding target behaviors on the DRC, and typically some reward is provided contingent on the child's performance." This meta-analysis evaluated the DRC alone (not within multi-modal packages) for students with ADHD across 14 single-case studies.
requirements: Target behaviors must be operationalized with specific criteria for meeting each behavioral goal
Teachers provide feedback on the DRC and rewards are typically contingent on performance
Must be implemented in a school or primarily academic setting as studied here
constraints: Support in this synthesis is for students under 18 identified as having ADHD in school settings using the DRC as a stand-alone intervention
target_learners: Students with ADHD under age 18 in elementary and secondary school settings
target_learning_goals: Increasing on-task behavior and homework completion
examples: The meta-analysis included 14 papers with 40 single-subject cases published 1975-2013, coding 1570 data points from graphed time series.
key_sources: Pyle, K. K., & Fabiano, G. A. (2017). Daily Report Card Intervention and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Single-Case Studies. Manuscript submitted to Exceptional Children October 2016; accepted March 2017. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED583708

article_title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Qin Yongjie, Wang Yungui, Floden Robert E. (2016). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1159/000449036
title: Dundee Ready Education Environment Measure (DREEM)
description: DREEM is a standardized instrument for evaluating the medical educational environment, developed at Dundee University Medical School in 1997 by an international Delphi panel. It contains "50 items" scored 0–4 on a 5-point scale, with nine negative items reverse-scored, so higher scores indicate a more positive evaluation; the maximum score of 200 represents an ideal environment. It includes five subscales covering perceptions of learning, teachers, academic self-perceptions, atmosphere, and social self-perceptions, and has been translated into at least nine languages. This review used DREEM as the sole outcome measure.
requirements: Reports mean difference and standard deviation of DREEM scores for intervention and control groups
constraints: Used here only for medical/nursing educational environments
target_learning_goals: perceptions of the medical educational environment
examples: All six included RCTs measured the educational environment with DREEM after the PBL or LBL intervention
key_sources: Qin Yongjie, Wang Yungui, Floden Robert E. (2016). The Effect of Problem-Based Learning on Improvement of the Medical Educational Environment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. https://doi.org/10.1159/000449036

article_title: A systematic review and analysis of the viability of virtual reality (VR) in construction work and education
citation: Zia Ud Din, Payam Mohammad, Rachael Sherman. (2024). A systematic review and analysis of the viability of virtual reality (VR) in construction work and education. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5059219
title: DroneSim: a VR-based flight training simulator for drone-mediated building inspections
description: DroneSim is a VR-based flight training simulator developed as an alternative to real-world drone-mediated building inspection training. The review reports it "enhanced construction stud ents' UAV operational and flight training skills" and acted as an efficient alternative to traditional real-world inspection training. It is presented as an example of VR for training in operating unmanned aerial vehicles for building inspections.
requirements: VR head-mounted hardware and simulation software to run flight training scenarios
target_learners: Construction students learning UAV-based building inspection
target_learning_goals: UAV operational and flight training skills for building inspections
examples: The review describes DroneSim as representing a virtual training group in the cited study
key_sources: Zia Ud Din, Payam Mohammad, Rachael Sherman. (2024). A systematic review and analysis of the viability of virtual reality (VR) in construction work and education. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5059219

article_title: Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety
citation: Mehmet Nuri Kardaş & Raşit Koç. (2017). Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety. International Journal of Progressive Education, 13(1). https://www.inased.org
title: Drama sessions structured in three stages: warm-up, impersonation, and assessment
description: The article describes drama activities as organized in a recurring three-stage session structure. In the warm-up stage students do physical and rhythm activities to get ready to express themselves and socialize; in the impersonation stage the selected activity is performed; in the assessment stage students reflect on their feelings to build awareness and empathy. The study's 8-week test-group program followed these stages meticulously.
requirements: Participants, a setting where players can comfortably express themselves, a subject/content, and a drama leader who provides continuity for the process
constraints: The leader should avoid going too far with the games and tiring the participants unnecessarily
examples: The test group's 8-week program used warm-up walking and harmonization exercises, improvisation plays such as The Chair of Dreams and I am a Presenter, and post-session relaxation exercises
key_sources: Mehmet Nuri Kardaş & Raşit Koç. (2017). Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety. International Journal of Progressive Education, 13(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131916

article_title: Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety
citation: Mehmet Nuri Kardaş & Raşit Koç. (2017). Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety. International Journal of Progressive Education, 13(1). https://www.inased.org
title: Drama as a multidimensional, student-centered instructional method for communication development
description: The article frames drama as a modern instructional method that is student-centered, learner-activated, hands-on, and entertaining, drawing on theatre techniques such as role playing, improvisation, role cards, and dramatization. It treats drama as "a mult i-dimensional concept" spanning education, visual arts, and psychological treatment, and argues that through drama activities students achieve thinking, speaking, listening, and narrative skills, with group interaction improving language skills naturally.
requirements: Student enthusiasm and willingness; development levels of students considered; a suitable setting; appropriate time without haste; each activity assessed after completion
constraints: The article states these conditions per the Ministry of National Education guidance for drama applications
target_learners: K-12 students, here 7th-grade Turkish language learners
examples: The researchers implemented eight improvisation-based plays over 8 weeks, with the researcher serving as drama leader in each play
key_sources: Mehmet Nuri Kardaş & Raşit Koç. (2017). Effect of Drama Instruction Method on Students' Turkish Verbal Skills and Speech Anxiety. International Journal of Progressive Education, 13(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1131916

article_title: Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess
citation: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Effects+of+the+Coordination+Exercise+Program+on+School+Children%27s+Agility
title: Droutability coordination exercise program with cross plates and colored numbered disks
description: The Droutability coordination exercise program, developed by Yasumitsu (2007), uses cross plates (24 cm × 24 cm) and colored disks 15 cm in diameter placed on half of a gymnasium floor. Students in two subgroups alternate 30-second activity bouts: they step quickly over a cross plate, then respond to a command such as a color or number by running to the matching disk, touching it with a foot, and returning to resume stepping. The experimental group completed "four sets of 30-second intervention activity in each intervention recess".
requirements: A gymnasium space with 16 cross plates and six sets of nine colored numbered disks (54 disks in total) randomly placed on half of the floor (15 m × 15 m)
A command-giver directing students to disks of specific colors or numbers
constraints: The intervention was delivered in 20-minute recess periods, two to three times a week for five weeks, totaling 12 intervention recesses
target_learning_goals: Improve agility, including quick direction changes, orientation ability, and reaction to commands
examples: In the study, students ran to a disk matching a commanded color or number, touched it with a foot, and returned to their cross plate, moving in all directions while avoiding collisions with classmates
key_sources: Tatsuo Yasumitsu, Haruo Nogawa, Yoshiro Hatano. (2012). Effects of the Coordination Exercise Program on School Children's Agility: Short-Time Program during School Recess. Journal of Research, volume 6, issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ954491

article_title: The Effect of Written Corrective Feedback on Grammatical Accuracy of EFL Students: An Improvement over Previous Unfocused Designs
citation: Mobin Khanlarzadeh, Majid Nemati. (2016). The effect of written corrective feedback on grammatical accuracy of EFL students: An improvement over previous unfocused designs. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 4(2). https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Draft-Specific Scoring (DSS) for motivating revision without feedback
description: Draft-Specific Scoring is a grading technique, devised by Nemati and Azizi (2013) and used in this study, in which learners are assured that if they improve their first drafts during revision, their task scores will be replaced by the revision scores. The article reports it "was also used to assure the students that if they improved upon their first drafts in the revision process, their scores on the writing tasks would change to those of revisions." It served to keep both groups, including the no-feedback control, motivated to revise seriously and addressed the ethical problem of giving feedback to one group only.
requirements: Instructor scores both drafts and revisions and replaces draft scores with revision scores when students improve
constraints: Used here with elementary EFL learners in a private language institute context
examples: Both groups were given scored drafts back to revise in class for possibly a better score, with no teacher or peer feedback allowed during revision.
key_sources: Mobin Khanlarzadeh, Majid Nemati. (2016). The effect of written corrective feedback on grammatical accuracy of EFL students: An improvement over previous unfocused designs. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 4(2). https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue Based on His Majesty the King's Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Chaemsai, R. & Rattanavich, S. (2016). The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue based on His Majesty the King’s Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students’ Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p18
title: Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA): a student-centered reading method built on a predicting-reading-proving cycle
description: DR-TA, created by Stauffer (1969) and adapted by Tierney et al. (1995), is a student-centered reading method in which "readers through guessing overall reading content before starting to read, are able to set their reading objectives" and then read and prove predictions in a repeating cycle. The teacher acts as a facilitator, "assisting students in connecting background knowledge and new information". The article applies it with tales of virtue texts to teach English reading comprehension while raising ethical awareness.
requirements: Students read segmented texts silently and are guided through prediction, silent reading, and proof questions with the teacher facilitating rather than lecturing
examples: In the study, the experimental group was taught through DR-TA for 10 weeks with 20 teaching hours using tales of virtue based on the King's teaching concepts

The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue based on His Majesty the King’s Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students’ Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p18
title: DR-TA instructional sequence: predicting, reading, and proving repeated per text segment, followed by fundamental skill training
description: The article describes a two-phase instructional pattern. Phase 1 directs the reading-thinking process through three steps — "Predicting", "Reading", and "Proving" — repeated "with each new segment" of text, with students closing their books for comprehension-check questions such as "Were you correct?". Phase 2 provides fundamental skill training, reexamining story elements to develop word attack, semantic analysis, concept clarification, observation, and reflective abilities.
requirements: Teacher directs students to study the title or pictures before reading and asks proof questions after each segment
target_learning_goals: word attack and reflective reading skills
examples: Students encountering unknown words follow a fixed order: read to the end of the sentence, use picture clues, sound out the word, then ask the teacher

article_title: Comparative Study between Drill Skill and Concept Attainment Model towards Physics Learning Achievement
citation: Izaak Hendrik Wenno, Pieter Wattimena, Luky Maspaitela. (2016). Comparative Study between Drill Skill and Concept Attainment Model towards Physics Learning Achievement. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol.5, No.3. http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Drill skill model as a teaching technique based on repeated training activities
description: The drill skill model is described as "a teaching technique in which students carry out training activities on what they have learned", so that material already taught becomes more embedded in students' minds and students develop higher dexterity or skills. In this study it was operationalized as the treatment for the first experimental group, involving active exercise and application of theory to practice with feedback. The authors cite prior work suggesting active exercise can improve absorption and support transfer of learning to new situations.
requirements: Requires students to carry out repeated training activities on previously learned material
constraints: The article notes not all learning models are always effective for all specific learning situations or particular subject matter
examples: Used as the treatment for group 1 in the quasi-experiment, resulting in no students in the fail category after treatment

title: drdoubleb.com: an interactive case platform simulating real-world diagnostics with IHC/FISH integration
description: Dr. Brett Baskovich's website drdoubleb.com is described as "a dynamic playground where participants can strengthen their skills through hands-on interaction". It features interactive cases integrating clinical history with whole-slide images, and participants can request additional tests such as immunohistochemistry or FISH, with results presented as WSIs requiring further interpretation to reach a diagnosis. Several SIAPeC Quiz questions (n=7, 25.9%) were based on this website and resembled routine clinical practice the most.
requirements: Whole-slide image viewing capability
A mechanism for participants to request ancillary tests and receive results as WSIs or images
target_learning_goals: Diagnostic reasoning integrating morphology, clinical information, and ancillary tests
examples: SIAPeC Quiz cases drawn from the site included alveolar soft part sarcoma, NUT carcinoma, and follicular lymphoma

article_title: Validation of the ICO-OCEX tool for competency-based assessment in ophthalmology residency programs.
citation: Gull Ambreen, Yasmin Rahila, Mahboob Usman, Golnik Karl C., Moin Muhammad. (2026). Validation of the ICO-OCEX tool for competency-based assessment in ophthalmology residency programs. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09154-2
title: The Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition structures the ICO-OCEX assessment framework
description: The article uses the Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition as its conceptual framework, guiding the development and validation of the ICO-OCEX formative assessment tool. The model maps three training levels (early, mid, senior) onto three Dreyfus stages (novice, beginner, competent), which correspond to the tool's three-point rating rubric. The authors state the tool 'ensures the systematic progression of residents through the Dreyfus stages, enabling them to acquire the competencies needed for autonomy and patient safety.'
requirements: Residents must be assessed at three distinct training levels corresponding to novice, beginner, and competent Dreyfus stages
constraints: The three-point rating scale may limit discrimination between adjacent performance levels compared with more granular milestone-based systems
target_learning_goals: Progressive acquisition of clinical competencies toward autonomy and patient safety

article_title: Sociodemographic, lifestyle, and educational environment factors associated with academic performance among Tunisian medical students: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Sridi Chayma, Aribi Mayssa, Lassoued Latifa, Kacem Imene, Chelly Farah, Belhadj Narjes, Fki Amene, Elleuch Nour, Chouchene Imed, Maoua Maher, Ben Dhiab Mohamed. (2026). Sociodemographic, lifestyle, and educational environment factors associated with academic performance among Tunisian medical students: a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08518-4
title: Validated French version of the Dundee Ready Education Environment Measure (DREEM)
description: The DREEM is a 50-item instrument assessing students' perceptions of their educational environment, used here in its validated French version. The article states it "consists of 50 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree), with a maximum total score of 200", comprising five subscales (SPL, SPT, ASP, SPA, SSSP) with published interpretation bands. In this sample, "internal consistency of the DREEM was excellent (Cronbach's α = 0.91 for the total score)", with subscale alphas from 0.70 to 0.85. Nine negatively worded items were reverse scored before analysis.
requirements: Administered as a self-administered questionnaire; scores interpreted according to McAleer and Roff bands (0–50 very poor to 151–200 excellent)
constraints: Measures perceptions of the educational environment, not objective environment quality; higher scores indicate more positive perceptions
target_learning_goals: Assessment of students' perceptions of the educational environment for quality assurance and improvement
examples: Used as the environment-perception measure in the FMSo cross-sectional survey of 701 medical students, distributed via the University Virtual Platform

article_title: Importance of future motivation for skill acquisition among medical students undergoing endoscopic forceps training.
citation: Kamimura Go, Maeda Koki, Aoki Masaya, Imamura Satomi, Morizono Shoichiro, Tokunaga Takuya, Umehara Tadashi, Harada-Takeda Aya, Nagata Toshiyuki, Ueda Kazuhiro. (2025). Importance of future motivation for skill acquisition among medical students undergoing endoscopic forceps training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07048-3
title: Dry laboratory endoscopic forceps time-trial task for medical students
description: A dry-laboratory training element in which students transfer rubber tubes between boxes using two endoscopic forceps while being timed. The article describes it: "We conducted time trials in which the time taken to transfer nine rubber tubes (5 mm thick and 1 cm long) from one box to another using two forceps was measured". Students practiced daily for two weeks, could practice as many times as possible, and the fastest time of the day was recorded; skill acquisition was defined as the difference in average times between halves.
requirements: A dry laboratory with endoscopic forceps, boxes, and nine rubber tubes (5 mm thick and 1 cm long) for the transfer task
constraints: Time-based improvement does not comprehensively reflect surgical proficiency, which also encompasses precision, safety, and technique, per the article
target_learning_goals: endoscopic forceps handling and manual dexterity
examples: 98 fourth-grade students at Kagoshima University trained daily for two weeks (5 days first half, 5 days second half) with daily fastest-time recording

title: DragonSkin silicone simulated tendon repair model
description: A simulated tendon repair model using DragonSkin (Smooth-On) platinum-cure silicone cast into an 8mm tube, repaired with 3:0 Ethibond suture using a two-strand modified Kessler technique. The article concludes "DragonSkin® silicone is an adaptable and valid material for simulated tendon repair models", being low cost and widely available.
requirements: Prepared by mixing two precipitant liquids under vacuum and casting into a mould
constraints: Did not handle or glide like human tendon (8% agreement)
Reviewed in isolation; user experience not compared with other materials

examples: Twelve participants repaired the model and rated it on five Likert-scale parameters

article_title: The impact of the educational environment on student engagement and academic performance in health professions education.
citation: Kassab Salah Eldin, Rathan Ramya, Taylor David C. M., Hamdy Hossam. (2024). The impact of the educational environment on student engagement and academic performance in health professions education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06270-9
title: Dundee Ready Education Environment Measure (DREEM) inventory
description: The DREEM is a 50-item self-report inventory assessing student perceptions of the educational environment in medical and health professions schools, organized into five subscales: Students' Perception of Teaching, Perception of Teachers, Academic Self-Perception, Perception of Atmosphere, and Social Self-Perception, rated on a 0–4 Likert scale. In this study it served as the measure of educational environment antecedents, with "an excellent internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.95". Its overall score of 200 is banded from very poor to excellent.
requirements: Respondents rate 50 statements on a 0–4 Likert scale; nine items require reverse coding
constraints: Items with mean scores of 2 or less indicate problematic areas requiring attention; the instrument measures perceptions, not objective environment features
target_learning_goals: assessing student perceptions of the educational environment to improve education quality
examples: In this study the sample's average DREEM sum score was 134.74 ± 29.07, interpreted as more positive than negative

title: Five-level Dreyfus scale used to rate surgical autonomy per procedure
description: The survey measured trainees' current subjective autonomy for each of the 40 procedures on the 5-point Dreyfus scale, which "evaluates competency to perform a procedure according to five levels": Level 1 show and tell, Level 2 active help, Level 3 passive help, Level 4 supervision only, and Level 5 expert (learner performs procedures and manages complications independently). Instructors separately rated expected competency on a 5-point Likert scale, and both groups rated potential risk if a procedure is performed by a noncompetent surgeon.
requirements: Ratings are subjective self-assessments by trainees rather than objective skill assessment
constraints: Competency was based on subjective assessments; the article notes it may not reflect the true surgical skills of the trainees
target_learning_goals: Self-assessed autonomy in performing core urological procedures
examples: Trainees rated each procedure's autonomy level, with junior, intermediate and senior PGY groups compared in Figure 2.

title: DRC five-competency framework for secondary nurses' clinical practice
description: The DRC Ministry of Public Health requires secondary nurses to hold five competencies for clinical practice. The article states: "Secondary nurses in the DRC must have five competencies for clinical practice: (1) establishing professional communication, (2) making decisions about health problems, (3) performing nursing interventions, (4) managing resources, and (5) engaging in professional development." The study's qualitative analysis matched its nine themes to these five competencies, and CBE programmes allocate 358 h over four years to integrate them into optimal care.
requirements: Nursing students must acquire skills such as collecting patient data, identifying the patient's health problems, and planning a nursing care plan
examples: The MoH issued a 2005 ministerial decree introducing CBE in secondary nursing education institutions to provide secondary nurses with these competencies for providing PHC.

article_title: Effect of an endodontic e-learning application on students' performance during their first root canal treatment on real patients: a pilot study.
citation: Färber Christoph Maria, Lemos Martin, Said Yekta-Michael Sareh. (2022). Effect of an endodontic e-learning application on students’ performance during their first root canal treatment on real patients: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03463-y
title: DRSK RCT translucent-root endodontic tooth model for preclinical practice
description: An endodontic tooth model developed by the department based on treatment errors observed over five years, optimized through extensive evaluations by students and instructors. Its "translucent roots" made performed procedures visible to students, helping them understand the impact of each treatment step. Instructional videos were produced for each tooth type represented by the models (incisor, premolar, molar), and students practiced on three artificial teeth before entering the clinical course.
requirements: Used as additional training aids in endodontic pre-course settings before entering the first clinical course
constraints: The study design did not distinguish between the effect of the e-learning application and the use of tooth models
target_learning_goals: root canal treatment manual skills before real-patient treatment
examples: Students performed practical exercises on three artificial teeth (incisor, premolar, molar) before the clinical course; the authors state the exclusive use of an e-learning tool without artificial-teeth training may not have yielded the positive results
